flashcards.q: What is the direct mechanical parallel between tf.function's retracing and torch.compile's recompilation?
flashcards.a: tf.function traces a graph on first call with a given input signature (shape/dtype) and retraces on an incompatible signature -- mechanically identical to Dynamo's guards triggering recompilation on a shape/dtype/value mismatch.

flashcards.q: How is a 'recompilation storm' avoided in both tf.function and torch.compile?
flashcards.a: tf.function: specify an explicit relaxed input_signature (e.g. None for a dynamic dimension). torch.compile: mark dimensions dynamic. Both compile once for a range of shapes instead of once per exact shape.

flashcards.q: What role does XLA play, and how does it differ in being opt-in (TF) vs default (JAX)?
flashcards.a: XLA lowers a traced graph into fused, hardware-specific compiled code -- the same role Inductor plays for torch.compile. TF: opt-in via model.compile(jit_compile=True). JAX: XLA compilation (jax.jit) is the default, always-on execution mode, reflecting JAX's functional, compile-first design.

flashcards.q: What does Keras 3 genuinely decouple that neither TF nor PyTorch offered independently before?
flashcards.a: The modeling API from the execution backend -- identical model code runs on TensorFlow, JAX, PyTorch, or OpenVINO (inference) via KERAS_BACKEND. Before Keras 3, Keras meant TensorFlow-only.
Using a backend-specific operation (e.g. a raw tf.* call) inside a custom layer/loss instead of the backend-agnostic keras.ops.* API.

flashcards.q: Why is TF Serving's batching described as request-level/static, and why is that a poor architectural fit for LLM autoregressive generation?
flashcards.a: batching_params.pbtxt groups whole, complete requests into one Session::Run() call -- fine for fixed-length workloads but wastes GPU cycles once shorter requests finish and wait for the longest, exactly the problem continuous/iteration-level batching (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, TGI) solves by swapping requests at every decode step.

flashcards.q: Is TF Serving's request-level batching limitation for LLMs a tunable configuration issue or architectural?
flashcards.a: Architectural, not tunable -- TF Serving's batching operates at request/session-run granularity by design; true iteration-level batching requires a fundamentally different serving architecture at the decode-step granularity.

flashcards.q: How does tf.GradientTape compare mechanically to PyTorch's autograd?
flashcards.a: tf.GradientTape requires an explicit 'with' scope to record operations for differentiation (opt-in-by-scope); PyTorch tracks every op on requires_grad=True tensors by default, always-on, with opt-out via no_grad()/detach(). Both compute the same reverse-mode gradient via tape.gradient() vs .backward()+.grad.

flashcards.q: How does tf.distribute.MirroredStrategy relate to PyTorch's DDP?
flashcards.a: Same core pattern: full model replicated per device, forward/backward on each device's own data shard, gradients all-reduced/averaged across devices before an identical update is applied to every replica. TPUStrategy extends the same pattern to TPU hardware.

flashcards.q: A TensorFlow SavedModel needs to run in an environment with no TensorFlow runtime. What's the standard path?
flashcards.a: Export via ONNX (the framework-agnostic interchange format) and run it in the target environment's ONNX-compatible runtime -- SavedModel itself is TensorFlow-specific and meaningless to a non-TensorFlow runtime.

flashcards.q: Why did TF2 (2019) switch to eager-by-default execution?
flashcards.a: TF1.x required building a static graph with placeholders (no real values until a tf.Session ran it), a painful, hard-to-debug model directly contrasted against PyTorch's 2017 eager-by-default debut -- TF2's switch matched that ergonomic improvement.

flashcards.q: What is the risk of over-generalizing 'TensorFlow and PyTorch have converged on ergonomics' to 'they are operationally interchangeable for every workload'?
flashcards.a: The frameworks remain independently engineered with different maturity, tooling, and serving ecosystems -- e.g. TF Serving's request-level batching is a genuine, current limitation for LLM autoregressive serving versus PyTorch-ecosystem options like vLLM, despite ergonomic convergence at the modeling/training level.
